text.en: Asha felt a small tremor in class. "Why does the ground shake?" she asked.

The Earth has layers: the crust, mantle and core. The lithosphere includes Earth’s crust and rigid uppermost mantle. It is broken into large and small plates that move slowly. Plate tectonics explains the movement and interaction of these plates. Endogenetic processes arise from forces within Earth.
Plate movements cause earthquakes, volcanoes and the folding and faulting of rocks. Earthquakes start at the focus and the epicentre is the point above it on the surface. Volcanoes can release gases and ash, and some eruptions allow molten rock to flow at the surface as lava.
Fold mountains such as the Himalayas form where plates collide, and the Pacific Ring of Fire has many volcanoes and earthquakes.

Think of four interacting Earth spheres. The lithosphere includes rigid rock, the hydrosphere includes water, the atmosphere includes air, and the biosphere includes places where life exists.

board.text: Rock, water, air and life interact

text.en: The crust is thin compared with the mantle and core. Continental crust is typically thicker and less dense than oceanic crust.
Earthquake waves travel through the interior and can change speed or direction at boundaries. Their paths give evidence about layers beyond the reach of drilling.

board.text: Seismic waves give evidence about the interior

text.en: Most of the mantle is solid rock. Under high temperatures and pressures it can deform over long periods. The outer core is liquid and the inner core is solid.

board.text: Mantle mostly solid · outer core liquid

text.en: Most rocks are made of minerals. Igneous rocks form when molten material cools. Sedimentary rocks often form when sediments are deposited and held together.

board.text: Igneous: cooling · sedimentary: deposition and consolidation

text.en: Metamorphic rocks form when existing rock changes under heat, pressure or chemical conditions without fully melting. The same material can pass through different stages of the rock cycle.

board.text: Metamorphism changes rock without full melting

text.en: Internal forces can build or deform landforms. External processes such as weathering and erosion can reshape the same landforms over time.
At a divergent boundary, neighbouring plates move apart. Magma can rise into the gap and cool, making new oceanic crust at an ocean ridge.
At a convergent boundary, plates move toward each other. A denser oceanic plate can sink beneath another plate. This process is subduction.
When two continental regions collide, rock can fold and thicken. The ongoing collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates helped build the Himalayas.
At a transform boundary, plates slide past one another. Fault movement can release stored stress even without forming or destroying crust at the boundary.
When layers fold, an upward arch is an anticline and a downward bend is a syncline in a simple undeformed diagram. Some folds are much more complex.
Faulting occurs when rock breaks and blocks move relative to one another. Displacements along faults can raise or lower adjacent blocks.
A raised block between faults is called a horst. A lowered block is called a graben in a common schematic. Look at movement along the faults before naming the landform.
A fault can hold while stress builds. During an earthquake, sudden movement releases energy and sends seismic waves through Earth.

board.text: Sudden movement can release stored energy

text.en: The focus lies at the point inside Earth where rupture starts. The epicentre lies directly above it on the surface. They are positions on different levels.

board.text: Focus underground · epicentre on the surface

text.en: Magnitude describes the earthquake’s size at its source. Intensity describes how shaking is experienced at a particular place. One event can have different intensities in different places.
A tsunami can arise when a large disturbance displaces seawater. An undersea earthquake that shifts the seabed vertically is one possible cause. Many earthquakes do not produce tsunamis.

board.text: Water displacement can start a tsunami

text.en: Molten rock below the surface is magma. Molten rock that reaches the surface is lava. An eruption can also release ash and gases.

board.text: Magma below · lava at the surface

text.en: A shield volcano is broad and usually has gentler slopes. A stratovolcano is often steeper and can build from layers of lava and other material.
The Ring of Fire follows much of the edge of the Pacific Ocean, where several plates meet. It is a broad belt of volcanic and earthquake activity, rather than a single line.

board.text: Pacific margin: many active plate boundaries

text.en: An earthquake or volcano can also occur away from some plate boundaries. A hot-spot island chain is an example of volcanoes that may lie inside a plate.
Read a tectonic diagram by identifying the two sides and following their arrows. Infer how the blocks move, then compare the predicted landforms with the evidence shown.

board.text: Read motion first, then interpret the landform

problem.en: On a cross-section, a fault starts slipping below ground at point F. Point E is on the surface directly above it. Identify each point.

text.en: Locate where fault rupture starts.

why.en: The point below ground, F, is the focus.

text.en: Trace vertically upward from the focus to the surface.

why.en: The point directly above it, E, is the epicentre.

prompt.en: A friend says The epicentre is deep underground. How will you reply?

requiredIdeas.en: The epicentre is on the surface.

points.en: Tectonic plates are rigid pieces of lithosphere that move slowly.
